learning_objectives.description: Understand the exponential notation, distinguishing base and power, and apply sign rules for odd/even powers of negative rational numbers.
success_criteria: Identify base and exponent in exponential notation
Evaluate odd and even powers of negative numbers accurately

learning_objectives.description: Reason and apply the concept of negative integral exponents as multiplicative inverses and reciprocal fractions.
success_criteria: Transform negative exponents into reciprocal positive powers
Compute values of rational bases with negative powers

learning_objectives.description: Master and apply the 5 fundamental laws of exponents with integral powers to simplify complex numerical and algebraic expressions.
success_criteria: Execute product, quotient, and power of power laws correctly
Apply zero exponent identity a^0 = 1 for any non-zero base

learning_objectives.description: Solve exponential equations by transforming expressions to common bases and equating exponents.
success_criteria: Align LHS and RHS to identical prime or rational bases
Formulate and solve linear equations in the exponent variable

learning_objectives.description: Convert extreme astronomical and microscopic scientific measurements between usual decimal form and standard scientific notation.
success_criteria: Express numbers in standard form k * 10^n with 1 <= k < 10
Compare real-world physical dimensions and perform arithmetic on scientific numbers

concept_graph.name: Exponential Notation and Sign Rules
concept_graph.definition_raw: Repeated multiplication of a rational number by itself is expressed as exponential notation \(a^n\), where \(a\) is the base and \(n\) is the exponent or index. For any fraction, \((\frac{p}{q})^n = \frac{p^n}{q^n}\). A negative base raised to an odd power retains a negative value, whereas raised to an even power produces a positive value.
concept_graph.definition_math_insulated: Repeated multiplication of a rational number by itself is expressed as exponential notation \(a^n\), where \(a\) is the base and \(n\) is the exponent or index. For any fraction, \((\frac{p}{q})^n = \frac{p^n}{q^n}\). A negative base raised to an odd power retains a negative value, whereas raised to an even power produces a positive value.

concept_graph.name: Negative Integral Exponents and Reciprocals
concept_graph.definition_raw: A negative integral exponent indicates repeated division and represents the multiplicative inverse of the corresponding positive power: \(a^{-n} = \frac{1}{a^n}\). For any non-zero rational fraction, \((\frac{p}{q})^{-n} = (\frac{q}{p})^n\). The product of a non-zero number and its multiplicative inverse always equals 1.
concept_graph.definition_math_insulated: A negative integral exponent indicates repeated division and represents the multiplicative inverse of the corresponding positive power: \(a^{-n} = \frac{1}{a^n}\). For any non-zero rational fraction, \((\frac{p}{q})^{-n} = (\frac{q}{p})^n\). The product of a non-zero number and its multiplicative inverse always equals 1.

concept_graph.name: The Five Fundamental Laws of Exponents
concept_graph.definition_raw: For non-zero rational bases and integral exponents: (1) Product Law: \(a^m \times a^n = a^{m+n}\); (2) Quotient Law: \(a^m \div a^n = a^{m-n}\); (3) Power of a Power: \((a^m)^n = a^{mn}\); (4) Power of a Product: \(a^m \times b^m = (ab)^m\); and (5) Zero Exponent Law: \(a^0 = 1\) for every non-zero base \(a\).
concept_graph.definition_math_insulated: For non-zero rational bases and integral exponents: (1) Product Law: \(a^m \times a^n = a^{m+n}\); (2) Quotient Law: \(a^m \div a^n = a^{m-n}\); (3) Power of a Power: \((a^m)^n = a^{mn}\); (4) Power of a Product: \(a^m \times b^m = (ab)^m\); and (5) Zero Exponent Law: \(a^0 = 1\) for every non-zero base \(a\).

concept_graph.name: Solving Exponential Equations
concept_graph.definition_raw: An exponential equation contains an unknown variable in the exponent. When two exponential expressions with the same non-zero base (other than 1 or -1) are equal, their exponents must be equal: if \(a^x = a^y\), then \(x = y\). Unknown terms are isolated by aligning both sides to common bases.
concept_graph.definition_math_insulated: An exponential equation contains an unknown variable in the exponent. When two exponential expressions with the same non-zero base (other than 1 or -1) are equal, their exponents must be equal: if \(a^x = a^y\), then \(x = y\). Unknown terms are isolated by aligning both sides to common bases.

concept_graph.name: Standard Form and Scientific Notation
concept_graph.definition_raw: Scientific notation represents extreme numbers in the normalized form \(k \times 10^n\), where \(1 \le k < 10\) and \(n\) is an integer. For numbers smaller than 1, shifting the decimal point to the right produces a negative exponent \(n\). For numbers greater than 10, shifting to the left produces a positive exponent \(n\).
concept_graph.definition_math_insulated: Scientific notation represents extreme numbers in the normalized form \(k \times 10^n\), where \(1 \le k < 10\) and \(n\) is an integer. For numbers smaller than 1, shifting the decimal point to the right produces a negative exponent \(n\). For numbers greater than 10, shifting to the left produces a positive exponent \(n\).

misconceptions.name: Base Negation Error
misconceptions.description: Student confuses a negative exponent with a negative base value, assuming a negative power turns the whole number negative.
misconceptions.remediation_strategy: A negative sign in an exponent designates reciprocal division (multiplicative inverse), not an arithmetic negative sign on the base.

misconceptions.name: Base Multiplication Confusion
misconceptions.description: Student multiplies the bases together when applying the product law (e.g. treating 2^3 * 2^4 as 4^7).
misconceptions.remediation_strategy: When identical bases are multiplied, the base represents the unchanging factor; only the counts of factors (exponents) combine.

misconceptions.name: Quotient Exponent Division
misconceptions.description: Student divides exponents by each other during base division instead of subtracting them (e.g. treating 3^6 / 3^2 as 3^3).
misconceptions.remediation_strategy: Division of like bases cancels common factors one by one; therefore, denominator exponent count subtracts from numerator count.

misconceptions.name: Zero Power Value Confusion
misconceptions.description: Student assumes raising a non-zero base to power zero equals zero or equals the base itself.
misconceptions.remediation_strategy: By the quotient rule, dividing any non-zero quantity by itself yields an exponent difference of zero and an arithmetic value of 1.

misconceptions.name: Non-Normalized Coefficient Error
misconceptions.description: Student leaves multiple non-zero digits before the decimal point (e.g. writing 35 * 10^4 instead of 3.5 * 10^5).
misconceptions.remediation_strategy: Standard scientific notation requires the leading decimal coefficient to contain strictly one non-zero digit to the left of the point.

assessment_items.prompt: What is the value of \((-1)^7\)?
assessment_items.prompt_math_insulated: What is the value of \((-1)^7\)?

options.distractor_explanation: Correct choice.
Raising a negative unit base to an odd exponent retains a negative sign through unpaired factors.
Exponents represent repeated multiplication of the base, not multiplication of base with exponent.
Repeated multiplication of unit factors cannot increase the absolute numerical magnitude above one.

hints.H1_hook: Notice whether the exponent 7 is an even number or an odd number.
hints.H2_concept: An odd number of negative signs leaves one unpaired negative factor.
hints.H3_formula: Recall the rule: (-1) raised to any odd natural number retains its negative sign.
hints.H4_step: Multiplying negative one by itself seven times pairs three negatives into positives, leaving one negative.

assessment_items.prompt: Evaluate \(13^3\) into expanded standard value.
assessment_items.prompt_math_insulated: Evaluate \(13^3\) into expanded standard value.

options.distractor_explanation: Correct choice.
This value corresponds to 13 multiplied twice; a cube requires three factors of thirteen.
Multiplying base thirteen by the exponent three confuses repeated addition with repeated multiplication.
Carefully compute intermediate multiplication: 169 multiplied by 13.

hints.H1_hook: Identify the power: 13 raised to exponent 3 means 13 * 13 * 13.
hints.H3_formula: Now multiply the product 169 by 13 once more.

assessment_items.prompt: Which power notation correctly expresses \(-15,625\)?
assessment_items.prompt_math_insulated: Which power notation correctly expresses \(-15,625\)?

options.distractor_explanation: Correct choice.
An even exponent applied to a negative base creates a positive number rather than a negative quantity.
Multiplying five factors of negative five reaches negative 3,125.
Squaring negative twenty-five reaches positive 625.

hints.H1_hook: Observe the negative sign in the given number -15,625.
hints.H2_concept: A negative power result requires an odd exponent on a negative base.
hints.H4_step: Since the final value is negative, (-25)^3 preserves the negative sign.

assessment_items.prompt: What is the rational value of \(4^{-3}\)?
assessment_items.prompt_math_insulated: What is the rational value of \(4^{-3}\)?

options.distractor_explanation: Correct choice.
A negative sign in an exponent inverts the factor into a denominator; it does not turn the product negative.
A negative exponent represents reciprocal division rather than positive direct power.
With a positive base, reciprocal inversion retains positivity without introducing negative signs.

hints.H1_hook: Focus on the negative sign in the exponent -3.
hints.H3_formula: Invert the base into the denominator: 1 / 4^3.

assessment_items.prompt: Express \((\frac{5}{3})^{-3}\) as a rational number of the form \(\frac{p}{q}\).
assessment_items.prompt_math_insulated: Express \((\frac{5}{3})^{-3}\) as a rational number of the form \(\frac{p}{q}\).

options.distractor_explanation: Correct choice.
The negative exponent indicates fractional inversion; both numerator and denominator remain positive.
Invert the fraction to remove the negative exponent before cubing numerator and denominator.
Exponents indicate repeated multiplication, not multiplication of numerator and denominator by three.

hints.H1_hook: Observe the negative exponent on the rational fraction (5/3).

assessment_items.prompt: What is the value of \((5^0 - 7^0) \times 3^3 \div 6^0\)?
assessment_items.prompt_math_insulated: What is the value of \((5^0 - 7^0) \times 3^3 \div 6^0\)?

options.distractor_explanation: Correct choice.
Subtracting equal zero-power terms reduces the inner bracket to zero.
Parentheses evaluate to zero prior to subsequent multiplication.
The term inside parentheses evaluates to 1 - 1, which completely eliminates the factor.

hints.H1_hook: Look at the terms raised to exponent 0: 5^0 and 7^0.
hints.H2_concept: Recall the zero exponent law: any non-zero base to power zero equals 1.
hints.H4_step: Multiply zero by any finite power product.

assessment_items.prompt: Simplify and express as a single power: \(9^5 \times 6^5\).
assessment_items.prompt_math_insulated: Simplify and express as a single power: \(9^5 \times 6^5\).

options.distractor_explanation: Correct choice.
When bases differ but exponents match, exponents do not add; bases multiply under the shared exponent.
Bases undergo multiplication under a common power, rather than basic addition.
Both bases must multiply, and the shared exponent stays unchanged.

hints.H1_hook: Notice that both factors share the exact same exponent 5.
hints.H2_concept: Recall the common power law: a^m * b^m = (ab)^m.
hints.H3_formula: Combine the bases under a single exponent: (9 * 6)^5.

assessment_items.prompt: Simplify the sum of reciprocal powers: \((\frac{1}{2})^{-2} + (\frac{1}{3})^{-2} + (\frac{1}{4})^{-2}\).
assessment_items.prompt_math_insulated: Simplify the sum of reciprocal powers: \((\frac{1}{2})^{-2} + (\frac{1}{3})^{-2} + (\frac{1}{4})^{-2}\).

options.distractor_explanation: Correct choice.
Inverting each unit fraction turns each denominator into an integer before squaring.
Squaring 2, 3, and 4 generates separate terms that sum together.
Negative exponents invert positive fractions into positive integers; no negative signs enter.

hints.H1_hook: Invert each fraction first: (1/a)^(-2) = a^2.
hints.H2_concept: Calculate the three squared integers: 2^2, 3^2, and 4^2.

options.distractor_explanation: Correct choice.
Do not forget the outermost exponent -1, which inverts the bracketed sum.
Add both reciprocal fractions using their common denominator six.
Compute 1/6 + 2/3 = 5/6, then take the reciprocal.

hints.H1_hook: Evaluate the two inner terms: 6^(-1) = 1/6 and (3/2)^(-1) = 2/3.
hints.H2_concept: Find a common denominator to add the inner fractions: 1/6 + 4/6.

assessment_items.prompt: By what number should \((-6)^{-1}\) be multiplied so that the product becomes \(15^{-1}\)?
assessment_items.prompt_math_insulated: By what number should \((-6)^{-1}\) be multiplied so that the product becomes \(15^{-1}\)?

options.distractor_explanation: Correct choice.
Dividing a positive target fraction by a negative factor leaves a negative quotient.
Invert the divisor when converting division to multiplication.
Divide the product by the known factor rather than multiplying them together.

hints.H1_hook: Set up the equation: (-6)^(-1) * y = 15^(-1).
hints.H4_step: Simplify -6/15 by dividing numerator and denominator by 3.

assessment_items.prompt: What number should be multiplied with \(5^{-3}\) so that the product becomes \(125\)?
assessment_items.prompt_math_insulated: What number should be multiplied with \(5^{-3}\) so that the product becomes \(125\)?

options.distractor_explanation: Correct choice.
Multiplying by one retains the reciprocal fraction rather than reaching the target whole number.
Multiplying opposite powers cancels to 5^0 = 1, not the target power.
A negative power of five decreases the numerical value further into smaller decimals.

hints.H1_hook: Write 125 as a power of 5: 125 = 5^3.

options.distractor_explanation: Correct choice.
Summing negative exponents -5 and -11 keeps a negative sign.
Remember to divide the combined exponent -16 by the coefficient 8.
Equate the sum of left exponents directly to 8x.

hints.H1_hook: Apply the product law to the left-hand side: add exponents -5 and -11.

options.distractor_explanation: Correct choice.
Be attentive with signs when isolating variable terms across the equals sign.
Subtracting positive 8 from -19 reaches -27; then isolate the variable term.
Divide -28 by -2 to find x.

hints.H1_hook: Apply the quotient law to the LHS: subtract the denominator exponent: -19 - 8.
hints.H4_step: Subtract 1 from both sides to get -2x = -28, then divide by -2.

assessment_items.prompt: Express the decimal \(0.000000000086\) in standard scientific form.
assessment_items.prompt_math_insulated: Express the decimal \(0.000000000086\) in standard scientific form.

options.distractor_explanation: Correct choice.
The leading factor in scientific notation must have only one non-zero digit before the decimal point.
Decimals smaller than one require negative exponents of base ten.
The coefficient must be greater than or equal to one.

hints.H1_hook: Locate the first non-zero digit: 8.
hints.H2_concept: Place the decimal point immediately after 8 to get 8.6.
hints.H3_formula: Count how many places the decimal shifts to the right from original position to 8.6.
hints.H4_step: Shifting 11 places to the right gives an exponent of -11.

assessment_items.prompt: Write \(3.05 \times 10^{-6}\) in usual decimal form.
assessment_items.prompt_math_insulated: Write \(3.05 \times 10^{-6}\) in usual decimal form.

options.distractor_explanation: Correct choice.
Ensure decimal shifts account for the single whole digit.
A negative exponent shifts the decimal point leftward, creating a small decimal fraction.
Moving 6 places left shifts past the digit 3 plus five additional zero placeholders.

hints.H1_hook: Observe the exponent -6: move the decimal point 6 places to the left.
hints.H2_concept: Moving one place left passes digit 3: .305.
hints.H3_formula: The remaining 5 shifts require inserting 5 zeros before 3.

options.distractor_explanation: Correct choice.
Factor out the lowest power 2^1999 from both numerator and denominator.
Exponents cannot be subtracted across fraction bars without factoring out common base multiples.
Calculate bracket terms after factoring: (4 + 1) / (2 - 1).

hints.H1_hook: Notice the common base 2 and very close exponent values: 1999, 2000, 2001.
hints.H2_concept: Factor out 2^1999 from both numerator and denominator.

assessment_items.prompt: When simplified, the algebraic expression \(x^{-1} + y^{-1}\) is equal to:
assessment_items.prompt_math_insulated: When simplified, the algebraic expression \(x^{-1} + y^{-1}\) is equal to:

options.distractor_explanation: Correct choice.
Negative exponents invert variables into denominators before addition.
Fraction addition retains separate denominator relationships.
Adding 1/x + 1/y requires cross-multiplying numerators over common denominator xy.

hints.H1_hook: Rewrite each term with positive exponents: 1/x + 1/y.
hints.H2_concept: Identify the common denominator for adding fractions with denominators x and y.
hints.H4_step: Combine the numerators over the common denominator.

assessment_items.prompt: Find the numerical value of \(x + x(x^x)\) when \(x = 2\).
assessment_items.prompt_math_insulated: Find the numerical value of \(x + x(x^x)\) when \(x = 2\).

options.distractor_explanation: Correct choice.
Follow order of operations: evaluate innermost power 2^2 first, then multiply by 2, then add 2.
Carefully compute: 2 + 2 * (2^2) = 2 + 2 * 4.
Do not add the outer terms before completing multiplication.

hints.H1_hook: Substitute x = 2 into the expression: 2 + 2 * (2^2).

assessment_items.prompt: What is the multiplicative inverse of \(10^{-100}\)?
assessment_items.prompt_math_insulated: What is the multiplicative inverse of \(10^{-100}\)?

options.distractor_explanation: Correct choice.
Multiplying a number by itself does not equal 1 unless the power exponent cancels to zero.
The multiplicative inverse inverts exponent sign; it never negates the base.
Adding -50 to -100 does not equal zero.

hints.H1_hook: Recall the definition: the product of a number and its multiplicative inverse must equal 1.

options.distractor_explanation: Correct choice.
Ensure all three terms are calculated and included in the sum.
Check the zero power term: any non-zero fraction to power zero equals one.
Sum the three evaluated components accurately without omitting terms.

hints.H1_hook: Apply power of power to the first term: (3^2)^3 = 3^(2 * 3) = 3^6.

assessment_items.prompt: If \(\frac{10}{3} \times 3^x - 3^{x-1} = 81\), find the value of \(x\).
assessment_items.prompt_math_insulated: If \(\frac{10}{3} \times 3^x - 3^{x-1} = 81\), find the value of \(x\).

options.distractor_explanation: Correct choice.
Factor out the common variable term before equating with the target power.
Equate exponents after converting both sides to identical bases.
Carefully isolate the variable term across the equals sign.

hints.H3_formula: Simplify the LHS: 3^(x + 1). Write 81 as base 3: 81 = 3^4.

assessment_items.prompt: What is the reciprocal of the rational number \((\frac{3}{2})^{-2} \div (\frac{1}{3})^{-3}\)?
assessment_items.prompt_math_insulated: What is the reciprocal of the rational number \((\frac{3}{2})^{-2} \div (\frac{1}{3})^{-3}\)?

options.distractor_explanation: Correct choice.
Remember to invert the final rational quotient to obtain the requested reciprocal.
Calculate 9 * 27 for the inverted product.
Carefully compute (2/3)^2 / 3^3 = (4/9) / 27.

hints.H4_step: Take the reciprocal of 4/243 by inverting numerator and denominator.

assessment_items.prompt: If \([((\frac{1}{3})^{-1} - (\frac{1}{4})^{-1})^{-1}]^m = 1\), what is the least positive integral value of \(m\)?
assessment_items.prompt_math_insulated: If \([((\frac{1}{3})^{-1} - (\frac{1}{4})^{-1})^{-1}]^m = 1\), what is the least positive integral value of \(m\)?

options.distractor_explanation: Correct choice.
An odd power on base -1 preserves a negative value.
The problem explicitly asks for the least positive integer (greater than zero).
An odd exponent preserves the negative sign on base -1.

hints.H1_hook: Evaluate the inner terms: (1/3)^(-1) = 3 and (1/4)^(-1) = 4.
hints.H3_formula: Take reciprocal: (-1)^(-1) = -1. The expression simplifies to (-1)^m = 1.
hints.H4_step: Recall that (-1) raised to an even power equals 1; the smallest positive even integer is 2.

assessment_items.prompt: Prove the algebraic identity: \(\frac{1}{1 + x^{q-p}} + \frac{1}{1 + x^{p-q}}\). What does it simplify to?
assessment_items.prompt_math_insulated: Prove the algebraic identity: \(\frac{1}{1 + x^{q-p}} + \frac{1}{1 + x^{p-q}}\). What does it simplify to?

options.distractor_explanation: Correct choice.
Express the negative index difference as a reciprocal fraction to establish matching denominators.
Multiply numerator and denominator of the second term by x^q to align denominators.
Summing the unified fractions forms (x^p + x^q) / (x^p + x^q) = 1.

hints.H1_hook: Express x^(p-q) as 1 / x^(q-p).
hints.H2_concept: Substitute into the second fraction: 1 / [1 + 1 / x^(q-p)].
hints.H3_formula: Multiply numerator and denominator of second term by x^(q-p).
hints.H4_step: Add the two fractions with identical denominators: [1 + x^(q-p)] / [1 + x^(q-p)].

assessment_items.prompt: A spacecraft travels at \(12\text{ km/s} = 1.2 \times 10^4\text{ m/s}\). If distance to Moon is \(3.48 \times 10^8\text{ m}\), how much time is required to reach the Moon?
assessment_items.prompt_math_insulated: A spacecraft travels at \(12\text{ km/s} = 1.2 \times 10^4\text{ m/s}\). If distance to Moon is \(3.48 \times 10^8\text{ m}\), how much time is required to reach the Moon?

options.distractor_explanation: Correct choice.
Divide exponents of ten: 10^8 / 10^4 = 10^(8 - 4) = 10^4.
Time equals distance divided by speed, not distance multiplied by speed.
Direct coefficient division leaves the base value unchanged while powers of ten subtract directly.

hints.H1_hook: Apply the physics formula: Time = Distance / Speed.
